title: Bounded Parallelism in Go Worker Pools: Semaphore Mechanics, Backpressure Propagation, and the Starvation Boundary
description: How Go semaphores, channel backpressure, and worker pool sizing interact to prevent goroutine explosion and starvation in production services.
linkedin_post:
Most goroutine explosion failures in production Go services don't look like crashes. They look like degraded latency under load spikes, invisible queue growth, and downstream resource saturation that appears before any individual call fails.

The root cause is usually the same: backpressure escapes at a goroutine spawn boundary. A loop that creates goroutines to avoid blocking on a channel is correct in isolation and catastrophic under sustained overload.

In a new article, I've written in depth about how bounded parallelism actually works in production Go services:

→ Why a fixed worker pool with WaitGroup doesn't bound memory under overload
→ How semaphore.Acquire becomes the backpressure point in fan-out patterns, and why the error channel buffer size matters
→ The pipeline backpressure directionality problem: why one goroutine-per-item breaks the entire chain
→ Starvation at the priority boundary, and why partitioned semaphores are a structural fix rather than a scheduling gamble
→ How to size a worker bound to downstream resource capacity instead of defaulting to GOMAXPROCS
→ Four observability signals that distinguish saturation, slowdown, and goroutine leaks

This is production-focused: failure modes, sizing arithmetic, and a concrete decision framework for choosing between pool, semaphore, and partitioned approaches.
